Hybrid between biologically and quantum-inspired many-body states

Miha Srdinšek Email: mihasrdinsek@gmail.com Affiliation: Université Grenoble Alpes, CEA, Grenoble INP, IRIG, Pheliqs, F-38000 Grenoble, France    Xavier Waintal Affiliation: Université Grenoble Alpes, CEA, Grenoble INP, IRIG, Pheliqs, F-38000 Grenoble, France
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Deep neural networks can represent very different sorts of functions, including complex quantum many-body states. Tensor networks can also represent these states, have more structure and are easier to optimize. However, they can be prohibitively costly computationally in two or higher dimensions. Here, we propose a generalization of the perceptron – the perceptrain – which borrows features from the two different formalisms. We construct variational many-body ansatz from a simple network of perceptrains. The network can be thought of as a neural network with a few distinct features inherited from tensor networks. These include efficient local optimization akin to the density matrix renormalization algorithm, instead of optimizing all the parameters at once; the possibility to dynamically increase the number of parameters during the optimization; the possibility to compress the state; and a structure that remains quantum-inspired. We showcase the ansatz using a combination of variational Monte Carlo (VMC) and Green function Monte Carlo (GFMC) on a 10×1010\times 10 transverse field quantum Ising model with a long-range 1/r61/r^{6} antiferromagnetic interaction. The model corresponds to the Rydberg (cold) atoms platform proposed for quantum annealing. We consistently find a very high relative accuracy for the ground state energy, around 10−510^{-5} for VMC and 10−610^{-6} for GFMC in all regimes of parameters, including in the vicinity of the quantum phase transition. We use very small ranks (∼2\sim 2-55) of perceptrains, as opposed to multiples of thousand used in matrix product states. The optimization of the energy was very robust. The entire phase diagram was found with a single initial condition and a fixed set of hyperparameters.

I Introduction

Two different sorts of networks are profoundly reshaping the landscape of numerical computations. On one hand, neural networks (biologically inspired) lie at the core of artificial intelligence [1]. On the other hand, tensor networks (quantum inspired), a natural framework for describing complex quantum states, are being increasingly applied in unrelated fields ranging from plasma physics to turbulence and optimization [2]. Very roughly speaking, neural networks promise generality and an algorithmic paradigm shift, since a large part of the learning process is still not understood. They seem to have a boundless range of applications. Instead, tensor networks promise access to exponentially large objects in a highly structured way. They are built on a well understood data compression, based on entanglement. Tensor networks are perhaps less general than neural networks, but when they can be applied, their internal structure makes them much more powerful. The goal of this article is to explore hybrid networks that retain some of the interesting properties of tensor networks in exchange for some of the added generality of the neural networks.

More specifically, both types of networks have been highly successful as variational ansätze for describing the ground states of quantum many-body systems.

For one-dimensional (1D) systems, matrix product states (MPS), also known as tensor trains, together with the associated Density Matrix Renormalization Group algorithm (DMRG) [3, 4] have allowed one to essentially solve a number of problems with machine precision. MPS are the most studied tensor networks. Their extension to two dimensional (2D) systems, projected entangled-pair states (PEPS), are theoretically very promising but their practical application is hindered by a large computational cost [5], so that two dimensional systems remain in practice very challenging. One could say that these techniques are on the verge of being able to tackle 2D correlated systems [6, 7], a central goal of contemporary computational many-body physics.

Using neural networks to represent many-body states, the so-called neural network quantum states (NNQS), is much more recent, yet quite significant successes have been demonstrated [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. These ansätze are very general. The absence of tensor network structure means that one has to resort to Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) to sample the wave function and estimate its energy and gradient with respect to the ansatz parameters. The ground state is found through some variant of (noisy) gradient descent. Although these ansätze are believed to be general enough to capture the ground state accurately, the challenge is in the optimization which can become a very challenging task [17]. This is a consequence of the non-physicality, a.k.a. over-generality, of the ansatz, with up to hundreds of thousands of parameters. Also, the structure of the ansatz is typically fixed at the beginning of the calculation, and it is not straightforward to dynamically change the number of parameters of the ansatz [18], a feature at the root of the success of DMRG.

The hypothesis at the root of the present work is that variational ansätze used in VMC follow some sort of ”expressivity-trainability” duality: the more general (”expressivity”) the ansatz is, in terms of its (lack of) structure and bare number of parameters, the more likely it will be able to approach an arbitrary ground state, but at the cost of being more difficult to optimize (”trainability”). A precise version of this duality remains to be formulated, and its validity assessed. For the moment we should treat it simply as a guiding principle in the upcoming ansatz construction: there is probably some room between the rigid structure of MPS and the highly general neural networks such as transformers which are expressive enough to represent both a many-body ground state and a large language model. To try and address this interplay, we build what we shall call a ”perceptrain”, a sort of perceptron that uses internally a tensor train. Then we make a simple many-body ansatz by building a simple neural network of perceptrains. This work bears some similarities with other recent VMC calculations including tensor networks ansätze such as PEPS [19, 20, 21], tensorial neural networks (TNN) [22, 23], matrix product backflow states (MPBS) [24], MPS [19], and also with the so-called string bond states (SBS) ansatz [25, 26, 27].

The paper is structured as follows. In Sec. II we introduce the perceptrain and comment on the new features it brings to a network. In Sec. III we discuss how several perceptrains can be used to construct many-body wave functions. We propose a tailored optimization path for these ansätze, reminiscent of the DMRG algorithm. In Sec. IV we use the ansatz to solve a 10×1010\times 10 transverse field quantum Ising model. In Sec. V we explain more technical details about spontaneous symmetry breaking in VMC, our GFMC benchmark, and compare different optimization approaches. Finally, in Sec. VI we share our concluding remarks.

II From perceptron to perceptrain

II.1 Notations for perceptrons and MPS.

The basic building block of deep neural networks is the perceptron which mimics a biological neuron that ”fires” when its depolarization potential reaches a certain threshold. The perceptron is a non-linear function ϕ⁡(𝒙)\phi(\bm{x}) of nn real numbers 𝒙=(x1,x2,…,xn)\bm{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}), the inputs,

ϕ⁡(𝒙)=f⁡(𝑾⋅𝒙+b),\phi(\bm{x})=f(\bm{W}\cdot\bm{x}+b), (1)

where 𝑾\bm{W} is a vector of parameters (weights) and the additional parameter bb, the threshold (bias). The function f⁡(x)f(x) is typically the Fermi function (a common alternative being ReLU) mirrored along the y-axis (known as the logistic or sigmoid function in this context). Neural networks are constructed by chaining many network units (perceptrons), i.e. the output of one is used as the input of another.

The MPS is also a function of nn inputs that returns a scalar. However the input here is a vector 𝒔=(s1,s2,…,sn)\bm{s}=(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{n}) of indices that take discrete values: si∈{1,2,…,d}s_{i}\in\{1,2,...,d\}. The ”parameters” of the MPS are a set of n​dnd matrices AisiA_{i}^{s_{i}} and the MPS evaluates to,

ϕ𝒔=𝐓𝐫​A1s1​A2s2​…​Ansn.\phi_{\bm{s}}=\mathbf{Tr}A_{1}^{s_{1}}A_{2}^{s_{2}}...A_{n}^{s_{n}}. (2)

The size of the matrix AisiA_{i}^{s_{i}} is χi×χi+1\chi_{i}\times\chi_{i+1} where χi\chi_{i} is known as the bond dimension. By convention, χ1=χn=1\chi_{1}=\chi_{n}=1 so the first and last matrices are in fact vectors. The schematic of MPS is shown in Fig. 1b.

II.2 Perceptrain construction.

The perceptrain corresponds to replacing the inner function 𝑾⋅𝒙\bm{W}\cdot\bm{x} of the perceptron with an MPS. To fully replace perceptrons, we define a generalization of the MPS, which may take continuous values as an input.

The generalization can be done in many ways. Here we choose to expand the perceptrain on a basis of Chebyshev polynomials Ts​(x)T_{s}(x) of the first kind. Since these polynomials are well behaved for inputs inside the interval x∈[−1,+1]x\in[-1,+1], we use the hyperbolic tangent to convert the output of perceptrains to this interval. The overall network unit function in the continuum reads,

ϕ⁡(𝒙)=𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐡⁡[b+β​∑𝒔ϕ𝒔​Ts1​(x1)​Ts2​(x2)​…​Tsn​(xn)]\phi(\bm{x})=\mathbf{tanh}\left[b+\beta\sum_{\bm{s}}\phi_{\bm{s}}T_{s_{1}}(x_{1})T_{s_{2}}(x_{2})...T_{s_{n}}(x_{n})\right] (3)

where ϕ𝒔\phi_{\bm{s}} is an MPS and β\beta and bb are two additional parameters. Introducing the continuous matrix function Ai​(x)A_{i}(x) as

Ai​(x)=∑sAis​Ts​(x),A_{i}(x)=\sum_{s}A_{i}^{s}T_{s}(x), (4)

the perceptrain can also be rewritten as

ϕ⁡(𝒙)=𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐡⁡[b+β​𝐓𝐫​A1​(x1)​A2​(x2)​…​An​(xn)].\phi(\bm{x})=\mathbf{tanh}\left[b+\beta\mathbf{Tr}A_{1}(x_{1})A_{2}(x_{2})...A_{n}(x_{n})\right]. (5)

The upper panel of Fig. 1 shows a schematic construction. A network unit (circular shape), is composed of an inner function (rounded rectangular shape) and an activation function (ff, or tanh\tanh, black dot). We distinguish three types of inner functions: the one of the perceptron 𝑾⋅𝒙\bm{W}\cdot\bm{x} [red, Figs. 1(a)], an MPS with discrete input values [blue, Figs. 1(b)] and an MPS with continuous input values (green, Figs. 1(c)). Note the different meanings associated with the left hand side and the right hand side of Figs. 1(b) and 1(c). The lines with arrows on the left hand side correspond to flows of values, while the legs of tensors represents their indices. If two tensors are connected with a leg (a line without an arrow), this represents a summation over the corresponding index. We refer to any network unit that contains a tensor train as the inner function, i.e. either Fig. 1(b) or Fig. 1(c), as a perceptrain.

As a first (toy) illustration of the perceptrain, we have used a single perceptron and a single perceptrain to perform a simple classification task in two dimensions (with artificial data). The results are shown in Fig. 2 for a small bond dimension χ=5\chi=5 and d=5d=5 with the symbols representing the data (filled or empty depending on the class) and the shaded regions the classification resulting from the perceptrain (left) and the perceptron (right). The comparison is, of course, not fair to the perceptron since they are seldom used outside of a network and the perceptrain has many more parameters. The number of parameters of the perceptrain scales as χ2​n​d\chi^{2}nd which reduces to χ​d\chi d in our n=2n=2 two dimensional toy example. This should be compared to e.g. a simple single-layer perceptron network whose number of parameters scales as l​nln, with ll being the depth of the layer. The point of this figure is to illustrate that a single perceptrain already has a large expressing power, comparable to the one of a small network.

II.3 Discussion

From a purely mathematical perspective, neural networks support two crucial features: evaluation (for a given 𝒙\bm{x}, one can easily compute ϕ⁡(𝒙)\phi(\bm{x})) and automatic differentiation (through the celebrated backward propagation algorithm, the cost to obtain the full gradient ∂ϕ⁡(𝒙)/∂𝑾\partial\phi(\bm{x})/\partial\bm{W} is roughly the same as one evaluation). At a more qualitative level, the fact that the perceptron is bio-inspired may make it well adapted to represent the type of data that brains can process.

The perceptrain, however, has the following set of properties that we will leverage on in the rest of the article:

  • •

    Evaluation is straightforward and amounts to nn matrix-vector multiplications for a total complexity O⁡(n​χ2)O(n\chi^{2}).

  • •

    Automatic differentiation is also straightforward. The gradient with respect to all matrices AisA_{i}^{s} can be computed for the same cost as the evaluation provided that (as in the backward propagation algorithm) one caches the intermediate matrix vectors product during the evaluation:

    ∂ϕ⁡(𝒙)∂[Ais]p​q\displaystyle\frac{\partial\phi(\bm{x})}{\partial[A_{i}^{s}]_{pq}} =Ts​(xi)​β​[1−ϕ​(𝒙)2]​[A1​(x1)​…​Ai−1​(xi−1)]p\displaystyle=T_{s}(x_{i})\beta[1-\phi(\bm{x})^{2}][A_{1}(x_{1})...A_{i-1}(x_{i-1})]_{p} (6)
    [Ai+1​(xi+1)​…​An​(xn)]q\displaystyle[A_{i+1}(x_{i+1})...A_{n}(x_{n})]_{q}
  • •

    Local updates. One of the properties at the origin of the success of MPS is that, even though a matrix AisA_{i}^{s} is ”local” in the sense of being associated with one variable sis_{i}, modifying it has a global impact on the full function. Algorithms such as DMRG only make local updates but nevertheless are capable of finding global minima very efficiently [28].

  • •

    Compression. An MPS can be efficiently compressed to lower the rank χ\chi while losing a minimum of information. This is done by performing a series of singular value decomposition (SVD) for each matrix AisA_{i}^{s} and truncating the matrices by ignoring the smallest singular values.

  • •

    Dynamic rank increase. Conversely, it is possible to dynamically increase the rank of an MPS so that it becomes gradually more expressive. This can be done by fusing two consecutive matrices introducing Bis​s′=Ais​Ai+1s′B_{i}^{ss^{\prime}}=A_{i}^{s}A_{i+1}^{s^{\prime}} and performing the optimization on Bis​s′B_{i}^{ss^{\prime}} instead of AisA_{i}^{s} and Ai+1s′A_{i+1}^{s^{\prime}}. In a second stage the MPS structure is recovered by performing an SVD of Bis​s′B_{i}^{ss^{\prime}}, increasing the rank in the process.

  • •

    Initialization. The recent development of the Tensor Cross Interpolation algorithm [29, 30, 2] allows one to initialize an MPS with a large class of functions.

  • •

    Quantum inspired instead of bio inspired. Last, MPS are natural structures to express many-body wave functions, so the perceptrain may be well adapted for VMC.

In the rest of this article, we use the perceptrain to build simple yet efficient many-body ansatz for VMC. We leave the exploration of its usefulness for other tasks to future works.

III Simple many-body ansatz with perceptrains

In this section, we construct a simple two-layer neural network of perceptrains, referred to as ”perceptrain network” (PN), that we shall use as a variational ansatz. It is a direct extension of MPS to address, in particular, two-dimensional systems. For the sake of concreteness, we focus on quantum spin models but the content of this section applies to fermionic models as well.

III.1 Variational Monte Carlo framework

We consider a configuration space that consists of VV 1/2-spins 𝒔=(s1,…​sV)\bm{s}=(s_{1},...s_{V}) with si∈±1s_{i}\in\pm 1. We seek the ground state of a Hamiltonian HH that can be very general; the only requirement at this stage is that for a given 𝒔\bm{s}, there exists only a small (typically O⁡(V)O(V)) number of configurations 𝒔′\bm{s^{\prime}} for which H𝒔​𝒔′≠0H_{\bm{s}\bm{s^{\prime}}}\neq 0. We construct a (unnormalized) variational wave function ψ𝒔=ψ𝒔​(𝜽)\psi_{\bm{s}}=\psi_{\bm{s}}(\bm{\theta}) that depends on a vector of parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} and seek to minimize its energy

E⁡(𝜽)=∑𝒔​𝒔′ψ𝒔∗​H𝒔​𝒔′​ψ𝒔′∑𝒔′′|ψ𝒔′′|2.E(\bm{\theta})=\frac{\sum_{\bm{s}\bm{s^{\prime}}}\psi_{\bm{s}}^{*}H_{\bm{s}\bm{s^{\prime}}}\psi_{\bm{s^{\prime}}}}{\sum_{\bm{s^{\prime\prime}}}|\psi_{\bm{s^{\prime\prime}}}|^{2}}. (7)

Introducing the local energy

e𝒔=1ψ𝒔​∑𝒔′H𝒔​𝒔′​ψ𝒔′,e_{\bm{s}}=\frac{1}{\psi_{\bm{s}}}\sum_{\bm{s^{\prime}}}H_{\bm{s}\bm{s^{\prime}}}\psi_{\bm{s^{\prime}}}, (8)

the energy can be recast into

E⁡(𝜽)=∑𝒔|ψ𝒔|2∑𝒔′′|ψ𝒔′′|2​e𝒔=⟨e𝒔⟩|ψ|2,E(\bm{\theta})=\sum_{\bm{s}}\frac{|\psi_{\bm{s}}|^{2}}{\sum_{\bm{s^{\prime\prime}}}|\psi_{\bm{s^{\prime\prime}}}|^{2}}e_{\bm{s}}=\langle e_{\bm{s}}\rangle_{|\psi|^{2}}, (9)

where the second equality means that the local energy needs to be averaged with respect to the probability distribution p𝒔=|ψ𝒔|2/∑𝒔′′|ψ𝒔′′|2p_{\bm{s}}=|\psi_{\bm{s}}|^{2}/\sum_{\bm{s^{\prime\prime}}}|\psi_{\bm{s^{\prime\prime}}}|^{2}. The appeal of this formulation comes from the fact that p𝒔p_{\bm{s}} can be sampled through Markov chain Monte Carlo (e.g. Metropolis algorithm) and the corresponding energy estimated as E⁡(𝜽)≈(1/M)​∑α=1Me𝒔𝜶E(\bm{\theta})\approx(1/M)\sum_{\alpha=1}^{M}e_{\bm{s_{\alpha}}} where MM is the number of samples [31]. A typical value used in most of this work is M=3200M=3200. A very nice property of VMC is that as ψ\psi approaches the actual ground state ψ0\psi^{0} of HH (with energy E0E_{0}), the local energy approaches e𝒔≈E0e_{\bm{s}}\approx E_{0}, i.e. the local energy does not depend on the configuration anymore. It follows that the error of the estimate of the energy, at fixed MM, decreases upon improving the wave function. Ideally, if one could construct ψ0\psi^{0} exactly, a single configuration 𝒔\bm{s} would be sufficient to obtain the energy exactly (in contrast to the quantum computer counterpart of VMC [32]).

III.2 Ansatz construction

We now proceed with the construction of the PN ansatz. The construction was motivated by remarking that MPS capture local correlations in 1D problems very well, because the MPS’s structure reflects the actual geometry of the problem. In 2D, the natural generalization is PEPS but the corresponding computational overhead quickly becomes prohibitive. We choose instead to construct a network that involves several MPS, each associated to a different ordering of the spins, so that spins that are close spatially are also close in the ansatz for at least one of those MPS (see Fig. 3).

More precisely, we use KK different MPS to build KK different ”child” perceptrains ϕca\phi^{a}_{c}, for a∈{1​…​K}a\in\{1...K\} (typically K=4K=4 in our numerics). Each child perceptrain is described by the nn matrices AisA_{i}^{s} and a permutation 𝝈\bm{\sigma} of the spins (the ”ordering” of the spins) such that 𝝈i=j\bm{\sigma}_{i}=j with i,j∈{1​…​V}i,j\in\{1...V\}. We implicitly assume the index aa in these objects, to avoid cumbersome notation. ϕca​(𝒔)\phi^{a}_{c}({\bm{s}}) then takes the form

ϕca​(𝒔)=𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐡⁡[bc+βc​𝐓𝐫​A1s𝝈1​A2s𝝈2​…​Ans𝝈V].\phi^{a}_{c}({\bm{s}})=\mathbf{tanh}[b_{c}+\beta_{c}\mathbf{Tr}A_{1}^{s_{\bm{\sigma}_{1}}}A_{2}^{s_{\bm{\sigma}_{2}}}...A_{n}^{s_{\bm{\sigma}_{V}}}]. (10)

The full network consists of KK ”child” perceptrains of rank χ\chi and one ”parent” (continuous) perceptrain ϕp\phi_{p} of rank χp\chi^{p}. The variational wave function reads

ψ𝒔=ϕp​(ϕc1​(𝒔),ϕc2​(𝒔)​…​ϕcK​(𝒔)).\psi_{\bm{s}}=\phi_{p}(\phi^{1}_{c}({\bm{s}}),\phi^{2}_{c}({\bm{s}})...\phi^{K}_{c}({\bm{s}})). (11)

We emphasize that evaluating ψ𝒔\psi_{\bm{s}} amounts to a few MPS contractions. It is therefore computationally cheap with a cost that scales as K​V​χ2KV\chi^{2}. Here, the two-dimensional nature of the problem has been incorporated using the different orderings of the sites (as shown Fig. 3), circumventing paying the exponentially large cost coming from contracting a genuine two-dimensional tensor network.

In the calculations performed in this manuscript, we worked with only two values of χp\chi^{p}, χp=2\chi^{p}=2 (PN) and χp=1\chi^{p}=1 (SBS limit). We call the case χp=1\chi^{p}=1 the ”SBS limit” since the corresponding PN ansatz reduces to the SBS ansatz developed previously [25, 26, 27], provided we choose bc=0b_{c}=0, and βc\beta_{c} to be small enough for the non-linearities to be ignored. We found empirically, for our studied system, that the increase of accuracy obtained when going from χp=1\chi^{p}=1 to χp=2\chi^{p}=2 was relatively modest and it was more effective to increase χ\chi, or, even better, KK. When setting K=1K=1 (the MPS limit), we chose the horizontal ordering (top one in Fig. 3). In the SBS limit, the main difference between our approach and the one of [25, 26] is that we perform the optimization locally as we shall discuss next.

III.3 Optimization procedure

In the spirit of the two-site DMRG algorithm, we perform the optimization by iterating over the different matrices of the different MPS, optimizing two consecutive matrices at a time. For each pair of matrices AiA_{i} and Ai+1A_{i+1} the algorithm is the following:

  1. (1)

    put the orthogonal center of the corresponding MPS at the position ii. See Refs. [28, 33] for a discussion of orthogonal centers in MPS. Fixing the orthogonal center provides several advantages: first it ”brings” information from other matrices down to the ones that are being optimized, thereby conferring the local optimization a more global nature; second, it provides a natural metric for the tensors being optimized since their L2L_{2} norm becomes the one of the full tensor (in that sense the corresponding gradient would be a natural gradient for a single MPS). Third, it fixes the ”gauge” freedom inherent to an MPS.

  2. (2)

    fuse AisA_{i}^{s} and Ai+1s′A_{i+1}^{s^{\prime}} into Bis​s′=Ais​Ai+1s′B_{i}^{ss^{\prime}}=A_{i}^{s}A_{i+1}^{s^{\prime}}.

  3. (3)

    Generate MM new samples by performing a few, typically one or two, Metropolis moves for each sample. These samples may be correlated with the previous ones but are not correlated between themselves, which is an important feature.

  4. (4)

    calculate the gradient ∂E/∂Bi\partial E/\partial B_{i}. This gradient can be estimated from the samples through,

    ∂𝜽E=2​[⟨e𝒔​𝒪𝒔𝜽⟩|ψ|2−E​⟨𝒪𝒔𝜽⟩|ψ|2],\partial_{\bm{\theta}}E=2[\langle e_{\bm{s}}\mathcal{O}^{\bm{\theta}}_{\bm{s}}\rangle_{|\psi|^{2}}-E\langle\mathcal{O}^{\bm{\theta}}_{\bm{s}}\rangle_{|\psi|^{2}}], (12)

    where 𝒪𝒔𝜽=∂𝜽ψ𝒔/ψ𝒔\mathcal{O}^{\bm{\theta}}_{\bm{s}}=\partial_{\bm{\theta}}\psi_{\bm{s}}/\psi_{\bm{s}} is the logarithmic derivative of ψ\psi at site 𝒔\bm{s}, over parameters 𝜽=Bi\bm{\theta}=B_{i}.

  5. (5)

    optimize BiB_{i} using some sort of gradient descent. Here we use two different options: either a normalized gradient descent,

    𝜽→𝜽−α​∂𝜽E‖∂𝜽E‖2\bm{\theta}\to\bm{\theta}-\alpha\frac{\partial_{\bm{\theta}}E}{\|\partial_{\bm{\theta}}E\|_{2}} (13)

    where α\alpha is the learning rate. Alternatively, we can use the so-called stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [34, 35, 36] update which corresponds to an imaginary time evolution projected within the variational subspace or equivalently to natural gradient descent with respect to the quantum geometric tensor [37],

    Si​j=⟨𝒪𝒔θi​𝒪𝒔θj⟩|ψ|2−⟨𝒪𝒔θi⟩|ψ|2​⟨𝒪𝒔θj⟩|ψ|2.S_{ij}=\langle\mathcal{O}_{\bm{s}}^{\theta_{i}}\mathcal{O}_{\bm{s}}^{\theta_{j}}\rangle_{|\psi|^{2}}-\langle\mathcal{O}_{\bm{s}}^{\theta_{i}}\rangle_{|\psi|^{2}}\langle\mathcal{O}_{\bm{s}}^{\theta_{j}}\rangle_{|\psi|^{2}}. (14)

    The SR update is

    𝜽→𝜽−α​S−1​∂𝜽E.\bm{\theta}\to\bm{\theta}-\alpha S^{-1}\partial_{\bm{\theta}}E. (15)

    In practice, the geometric tensor can become singular and must be regularized [38]. This is done by introducing a shift of its diagonal Si​i→Si​i+ϵ1​Si​i+ϵ2S_{ii}\to S_{ii}+\epsilon_{1}S_{ii}+\epsilon_{2}. Typical values of the regularization parameters that we used are ϵ1=0.01\epsilon_{1}=0.01 and ϵ2=0.001\epsilon_{2}=0.001. In practice, the SS matrix is not inverted, rather one solves for the corresponding linear problem. This step may be computationally costly when one performs the optimization with respect to all the parameters of the ansatz (see [17] for a mitigation strategy). However, in the present case, since we only optimize with respect to a small subset of parameters, this bottleneck is absent.

  6. (6)

    perform an SVD of [Bis​s′]a​a′[B_{i}^{ss^{\prime}}]_{aa^{\prime}} considered as a matrix with a,sa,s indexing its rows and a′,s′a^{\prime},s^{\prime} indexing its columns,

    [Bis​s′]a​a′=∑bUa​bs​λb​Vb​a′s′,[B_{i}^{ss^{\prime}}]_{aa^{\prime}}=\sum_{b}U_{ab}^{s}\lambda_{b}V_{ba^{\prime}}^{s^{\prime}}, (16)

    truncate λb\lambda_{b} to keep only the χ\chi largest singular values and update [Ais]a​b→Ua​bs[A_{i}^{s}]_{ab}\to U_{ab}^{s} and [Ai+1s′]b​a′→λb​Vb​a′s′[A_{i+1}^{s^{\prime}}]_{ba^{\prime}}\to\lambda_{b}V_{ba^{\prime}}^{s^{\prime}}. This step can be used to increase (or possibly decrease) the rank of the MPS.

The above sequence is repeated for all MPS and all adjacent pairs of matrices within an MPS. This forms a “sweep.” The precise order in which these pairs are optimized does not appear to be very relevant in our experience. In our numerical experiments for the ”2D model” (see Sec. IV), convergence of the optimization is usually reached within ∼150\sim 150 sweeps while 333333 sweeps form what we call one “Epoch.”

We have performed three different variants of the above optimization which we tag ”static,” ”dynamical-χ\chi,” and ”dynamical-KK” optimization, the merit of which will be discussed below. They are defined as

  • •

    ”static” means that we fix KK (K=4K=4) and χ\chi at the beginning of the calculation and optimize all parameters one after another.

  • •

    ”dynamical-χ\chi” means that we start with a low value of χ\chi, optimize the parameters, increase χ\chi [following step (6)] and then repeat the sequence until the targeted value of χ\chi has been reached.

  • •

    ”dynamical-KK” means that we start with all the children perceptrains initialized with the constant function and optimize only the K=1K=1 child perceptrain, then start to optimize the second child perceptrain (considering the first child as fixed), and continue the sequence until all child perceptrains have been optimized.

III.4 Scaling of the algorithm

We summarize here the scaling of the different parts of the algorithm. Evaluating an MPS for a single configuration takes nn matrix-vector multiplications, and hence scales as 𝒪⁡(χ2​n)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{2}n). The memory footprint is 2​χ2​n2\chi^{2}n. Putting an MPS in the canonical form uses the QR decomposition and therefore scales as 𝒪⁡(χ3​n)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{3}n). Taking the derivative of an MPS with respect to one tensor scales as one evaluation (MPS naturally implements automatic differentiation). Last, during an evaluation, one can cache the left and right partial contractions (the ”environments” of a site) making it possible to compute a new configuration where one spin is flipped with only 𝒪⁡(χ2)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{2}) (for the cost of doubling the memory footprint).

In the present context, the above translates into a single evaluation of ψ⁡(𝒔)\psi(\bm{s}) that scales as 𝒪⁡(K​V​χc2)\mathcal{O}(KV\chi_{c}^{2}). The cost of evaluating the “parent” perceptrain in our examples is negligible, and can be ignored. The rest of the scaling of the approach is Hamiltonian dependent and we specialize here to the transverse field Ising model described in the next section. The calculation of the local energy requires, for each configuration 𝒔\bm{s}, to calculate ψ⁡(𝒔′)\psi(\bm{s^{\prime}}) for all 𝒔′\bm{s^{\prime}} such that H𝒔′​𝒔≠0H_{\bm{s^{\prime}s}}\neq 0. In the present case, there are VV such neighbors. This in principle requires paying an additional factor VV. However, using the caching trick mentioned above, this factor can be avoided. Since we consider a long range model, the calculation of the diagonal energy itself H𝒔​𝒔H_{\bm{ss}} scales as V2V^{2}. Overall, for NoptN_{\text{opt}} optimization steps and MM samples, we arrive at a time complexity that scales as

C​P​U∼Nopt​(M​K​V​χc2+M​V2+K​V​χc3)CPU\sim N_{\text{opt}}\left(MKV\chi_{c}^{2}+MV^{2}+KV\chi_{c}^{3}\right) (17)

where in practice, the computing time is entirely dominated by the first term in the above equation. The memory footprint, however, consists of the MM configurations (M​VMV bits), the ansatz itself and a (optional) last term that corresponds to the caching, and dominates in practice

M​E​M∼M​V+K​V​χc2+M​K​V​χc2.MEM\sim MV+KV\chi_{c}^{2}+MKV\chi_{c}^{2}. (18)

For the typical numbers used in this work, the memory footprint is very mild, even using the caching.

IV Application to Transverse field spin model

We now turn to our numerical calculations where we focus on a transverse field Ising model in two dimensions. This model is interesting for its relative tractability, its link with quantum annealing experiments with Rydberg atoms and the absence of sign problem which allows us to verify the quality of our results using the post-VMC Green function Monte Carlo method (GFMC).

A rule of thumb with variational techniques is that a relatively accurate energy can correspond to very inaccurate physics. This is due to the energy being mostly controlled by relatively local physics while important long range behavior are associated with relatively small energy variations. It follows that a relatively poor variational ansatz may provide a correct equation of states but that one should be very careful with other observables than the energy. We shall illustrate this principle in our calculations with typically relative precisions better than 10−310^{-3} being needed to correctly capture the phase diagram. We shall also find that the accuracy correlates very well with the so-called ”VV-score,” which has been introduced recently [39].

IV.1 Model and its phase diagram.

We consider the transverse field quantum Ising model with VV sites. The Hamiltonian reads

H=∑i<jJi​j​σiz​σjz−hx​∑iσix.H=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}-h_{x}\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{x}. (19)

where σz\sigma^{z} and σx\sigma^{x} are the Pauli matrices and Ji​jJ_{ij} the exchange interaction matrix. A configuration 𝒔=(s1,s2,…,sV)\bm{s}=(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{V}) corresponds to the values of the spins along the zz axis so that

H𝒔​𝒔=∑i<jJi​j​si​sjH_{\bm{s}\bm{s}}=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}s_{i}s_{j} (20)

and for 𝒔≠𝒔′\bm{s}\neq\bm{s^{\prime}},

H𝒔​𝒔′=−hx∑a=1V…δsa−1​sa−1′δsa,−sa′δsa+1​sa+1′…H_{\bm{s}\bm{s^{\prime}}}=-h_{x}\sum_{a=1}^{V}...\delta_{s_{a-1}s_{a-1}^{\prime}}\delta_{s_{a},-s_{a}^{\prime}}\delta_{s_{a+1}s_{a+1}^{\prime}}... (21)

We perform almost all our calculations on a two dimensional system of V=10×10V=10\times 10 spins with open boundary conditions and an untruncated antiferromagnetic Ji​j=1/r6J_{ij}=1/r^{6} interaction where rr is the Euclidean distance between ii and jj on a square lattice with unit lattice spacing. In this setup the second nearest neighbor interacting term is 1/26=1/81/\sqrt{2}^{6}=1/8 of the nearest neighbor term, making this model mildly frustrated. The model can be directly mapped to the Rydberg atom quantum annealing model [40, 41, 42, 43] using a simple change of variables. We refer to this model as the ”2D model.” For benchmark purposes, we also considered a simpler exactly solvable one dimensional version, the ”1D model” of V=10V=10 sites with the interaction limited to nearest neighbors and periodic boundary conditions. Both models exhibit a quantum phase transition at finite transverse field hxh_{x} between an ordered phase and a paramagnetic phase [44]. Besides the energy, we will compute the following physical observables: the correlation function, the total staggered magnetization along the zz direction, and the total magnetization along the xx direction,

Ci​j\displaystyle C_{ij} =\displaystyle= ⟨σiz​σjz⟩=⟨si​sj⟩|ψ|2,\displaystyle\langle\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}\rangle=\langle s_{i}s_{j}\rangle_{|\psi|^{2}}, (22)
Mz\displaystyle M_{z} =\displaystyle= 1V​∑i=(ix,iy)(−1)ix+iy​⟨σiz⟩,\displaystyle\frac{1}{V}\sum_{i=(i_{x},i_{y})}(-1)^{i_{x}+i_{y}}\langle\sigma_{i}^{z}\rangle, (23)
Mx\displaystyle M_{x} =\displaystyle= 1V​∑i=(ix,iy)⟨σix⟩.\displaystyle\frac{1}{V}\sum_{i=(i_{x},i_{y})}\langle\sigma_{i}^{x}\rangle. (24)

Before exploring different aspects of our ansatz and optimization procedure, we quickly survey the final results that we obtained for the 2D model. Essentially, we find that, using our perceptrain based ansatz, we could solve the 2D model with an accuracy good enough to actually obtain the entire phase diagram, including the quantum critical point, in a reliable way. The results are shown in Fig. 4.

Figure 4(a) shows the obtained VMC energy versus hxh_{x} compared with our reference GFMC energy. At large field, E⁡(hx)→−N​hxE(h_{x})\to-Nh_{x} (all spins polarized along the xx axis) and at zero field E⁡(0)≈−1.5933​NE(0)\approx-1.5933N (classical limit). For the energy to remain within a narrow range as we vary hxh_{x} (so that features may be more visible), we plot the energy in the units of N​1+hx2N\sqrt{1+h_{x}^{2}}. We find a perfect agreement between VMC and GFMC in the whole range hx∈[0,10.]h_{x}\in[0,10.] (see Table 1 for a more quantitative statement). Zooming around E/(N​1+hx2)≈−1E/(N\sqrt{1+h_{x}^{2}})\approx-1, we see that the agreement remains up to at least the fourth digits.

Figure 4(b) shows the staggered magnetization MzM_{z} and the transverse magnetization MxM_{x} versus hxh_{x}. MzM_{z} acquires a finite value for hx<2.3h_{x}<2.3 where the system becomes antiferromagnetic. Conversely, MxM_{x} saturates in the paramagnetic phase for hx>2.3h_{x}>2.3 and is linear in the antiferromagnetic phase. The behavior of MxM_{x}, however, is much less sharp than the one of MzM_{z}. Here we computed MxM_{x} directly but it is fully consistent with the data of Fig. 4(a) using Mx=∂hxEM_{x}=\partial_{h_{x}}E and e.g. finite difference derivation.

The upper panels of Fig. 4 show the correlation function Ci​jC_{ij}. We observe, as expected, the development of strong antiferromagnetic correlations around the critical point in the window hx∈[2.2,2.5]h_{x}\in[2.2,2.5]. The goal of this article is the analysis of the capabilities of our perceptrain based ansatz, hence we shall stop here the study of the physics of the 2D model. It seems that our approach may be used as a very precise ”simulated quantum annealer,” but we differ the corresponding study to a subsequent publication.

IV.2 Perceptrain-based ansatz versus MPS in 2D

One of the chief motivations for our ansatz was to bypass the limitations of MPS ansatz in two dimensions. It is therefore crucial to show that, indeed, the perceptrain-based ansatz performs better than a simple MPS for the 2D model. The results are shown in Fig. 5(a). We find that we can consistently obtain relative accuracies better than 10−410^{-4} for very low bond dimensions χ∈[3−5]\chi\in[3-5] while regular MPS struggle to reach the 10−210^{-2} accuracy level even using larger bond dimensions. This is a very strong point in favor of our ansatz. Note that in DMRG, it is very common to use values of χ∼1000\chi\sim 1000, or even larger. Obtaining such high level of precision with such low bond dimension is a clear indication that the ansatz is particularly adapted to the 2D model. As expected, at a fixed rank (i.e. fixed level of expressivity), the precision decreases close to the criticality. However, increasing the rank consistently leads to higher and higher precision, allowing us to improve, if higher precision be desired. Figure 5(b) shows that our error level quickly improves with χ\chi as opposed to the corresponding MPS behavior. We also find that, in this regime, the SBS limit is almost as good as the full-fledged perceptrain based ansatz. Within our current setup, our accuracy appears to be limited to the ∼10−7\sim 10^{-7} level which we attribute to the remaining noise present using M=3200M=3200 walkers.

Figure 6 shows the same data but we plot the energy EE as a function of the variance of the energy var[H]=⟨H2⟩−E2[H]=\langle H^{2}\rangle-E^{2}. The variance is rescaled with respect to the size of the system and an estimate of the bandwidth of the energy spectrum, the so-called VV-score [39] which for our model evaluates to VV-score =N​var​H/E2=N\mathrm{var}H/E^{2}. As we shall see the VV-score is a very good proxy for the accuracy of the calculation. VV-scores in the 10−6−10−410^{-6}-10^{-4}, as obtained here, are considered of very high quality. This figure shows once again the large difference of ansatz quality between the MPS and the perceptrain ansatz (except for large value of hxh_{x} where the ground state eventually converges to a product state, i.e. a rank one MPS). We could, of course, push the rank of the MPS to much higher values. The point here is that with the perceptrain ansatz, an extremely low rank χ=2\chi=2 or 33 is sufficient to describe the ground state.

IV.3 Effect of the optimization path on the final precision

One of the hypotheses of this article is that the optimization path crucially affects the final accuracy that will be reached. More precisely, we surmise that the ability to dynamically increase the rank of the child perceptrains during optimization will make the optimization process more robust.

We now examine this hypothesis on our data. First, Fig. 7 shows two optimization procedures for the 1D model: a static optimization where the rank is fixed at χ=8\chi=8 at the beginning and a dynamical-χ\chi where we start at χ=2\chi=2, and increase the rank, until χ=8\chi=8 is reached. Since the system is small (V=10V=10 sites) we can also calculate the exact gradient of the energy without using VMC. When calculating the exact gradient, we find that the two paths converge to precisely the same accuracy (δ​E/E0≈10−5\delta E/E_{0}\approx 10^{-5}). However, when one uses VMC, hence noisy calculation of the gradient, we find that dynamical-χ\chi leads to a significantly better accuracy. It is more than one order of magnitude better compared to the static optimization. It is also interesting that in the case of dynamical-χ\chi, the exact gradient optimization and the noisy one follow each other very closely. In contrast, for the static optimization the noisy gradient converges significantly slower compared to the exact gradient. In plain words, the naive intuition that it is easier to find one’s bearings in a smaller space seems to be confirmed in this case.

Figure 8 shows a similar comparison of the optimization for the 2D model (where only the noisy gradient can be calculated). We find that dynamical-χ\chi (black) gives a result of slightly better quality. But more importantly, the direct optimization fails completely for χ=7\chi=7, while no such problem occurs in the case of dynamical-χ\chi. Actually, we find that there is a tiny loss of VV-score when we use dynamical-χ\chi up to χ=7\chi=7. We surmise that the additional parameters do not improve the expressivity much while making the energy landscape harder to navigate.

We conclude that adopting an optimization strategy similar to the two-site DMRG algorithm is actually robust and efficient for the studied model and the PN ansatz, despite the ansatz being significantly different from a simple MPS.

V Technical matters

In this last section, we give some technical details and highlight a few secondary findings. The model that we study presents a spontaneous symmetry breaking below a critical value of hxh_{x}. Section V.1 studies how our optimization process is affected by this spontaneous symmetry breaking. Rather surprisingly, we find that there exists a finite window of magnetic field where our ansatz is able to track both symmetry sectors simultaneously. Section V.2 presents the GFMC method that we used to obtain the reference values for the energies used earlier for error calculations. GFMC is in principle an exact (in the sense of unbiased) method, a fact which we check explicitly. Section V.3 looks at different variants of the gradient descent optimization. In contrast to neural network, we find that the optimization scheme is not crucial, although stochastic reconfiguration has slightly better performances. Section V.4 looks at how the presence of non-linearity of the ansatz affects the stability of the optimization.

V.1 Observing spontaneous symmetry breaking within VMC

We observe that the 2D model exhibits a quantum phase transition around hx≈2.4h_{x}\approx 2.4 (for the studied size). For hx=0h_{x}=0 the ground state is degenerate with two competing classical antiferromagnetic states. Switching all spins si→−sis_{i}\to-s_{i} maps one of these antiferromagnetic states (tagged 𝒔0\bm{s}_{0} below) onto the other (tagged 𝒔V\bm{s}_{V} below). Hence, strictly speaking, the staggered magnetization vanishes at all hxh_{x} due to the Z2Z_{2} symmetry si→−sis_{i}\to-s_{i}. The classical way to break this symmetry is to add a small (staggered) Zeeman field to the Hamiltonian.

Here, instead and mostly for the sake of curiosity, we do not break the Z2Z_{2} symmetry and study what happens during the optimization. To monitor the formation of a very large energy barrier between the two antiferromagnetic ground states, we consider a set of VV special configurations 𝒔f\bm{s}_{f} that contain ff spins in one antiferromagnetic state and V−fV-f spins in the other antiferromagnetic state with a domain wall in between, see the upper panel of Fig. 9 for illustration. Incrementally increasing 𝒔f\bm{s}_{f} corresponds to a sequence of single spin-flips (allowed by the Hamiltonian) that move the domain wall. The highest energy states along this path have V=10\sqrt{V}=10 nearest neighbor interactions that are frustrated (the domain wall). They form the macroscopic barrier between the two hx=0h_{x}=0 ground states. Figure 9(a) shows |ψ𝒔f/ψ𝒔0|2|\psi_{\bm{s}_{f}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2} versus ff while panel (b) shows |ψ𝒔V/ψ𝒔0|2|\psi_{\bm{s}_{V}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2} (red) and |ψ𝒔V/2/ψ𝒔0|2|\psi_{\bm{s}_{V/2}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2} (black) versus hxh_{x}. Very interestingly, we find that the optimization leads to three distinct regimes: for hx>2.4h_{x}>2.4, one is in the paramagnetic phase and the two symmetry sectors around f=0f=0 and f=Vf=V are equivalent |ψ𝒔V/ψ𝒔0|2≈1|\psi_{\bm{s}_{V}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2}\approx 1, meaning that one may ”freely” go from one sector to the other |ψ𝒔V/2/ψ𝒔0|2=O⁡(1)|\psi_{\bm{s}_{V/2}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2}=O(1). For hx<2.22h_{x}<2.22 the optimization has spontaneously chosen one symmetry sector, |ψ𝒔V/ψ𝒔0|2≈0|\psi_{\bm{s}_{V}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2}\approx 0 and |ψ𝒔V/2/ψ𝒔0|2≈0|\psi_{\bm{s}_{V/2}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2}\approx 0. For 2.22<hx<2.42.22<h_{x}<2.4, we are in a mixed regime: the two symmetry sectors are well separated |ψ𝒔V/2/ψ𝒔0|2≈0|\psi_{\bm{s}_{V/2}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2}\approx 0 but the wave function still captures both symmetry sectors |ψ𝒔V/ψ𝒔0|2≈1|\psi_{\bm{s}_{V}}/\psi_{\bm{s}_{0}}|^{2}\approx 1 [shaded gold region in Fig. 9b]. The fact that the wave function can track the two different hx=0h_{x}=0 ground states, although only for a finite window of magnetic fields, is quite promising for applications such as simulated quantum annealing. There, one would alternate optimization steps with a slow decrease of hxh_{x}, with the intent of finding the hx=0h_{x}=0 ground state, for a possibly highly frustrated Ising model.

The direct consequence of the existence of these three regimes is an hysteresis in the Mz​(hx)M_{z}(h_{x}) curve. Figure 9(c) shows the result of two calculations where all the walkers have been initialized in the 𝒔0\bm{s}_{0} configuration (red) or in the 𝒔V\bm{s}_{V} (yellow) configuration. After thermalization of the Metropolis Markov chain, the walkers remain trapped around the original configuration for 2.22<hx<2.42.22<h_{x}<2.4. In this regime a fully random initialization of the walkers (with 50%50\% of the walkers in each sector) would lead to a vanishing staggered magnetization (which is mathematically correct but physically wrong). This case is illustrated in Fig. 10. We observe that the magnetization initially grows but then eventually decreases. It is only when we start increasing the rank χ\chi that the optimization is able to recover the two symmetry sectors. To break the symmetry explicitly, the main results of Fig. 4 for MzM_{z} have been obtained by initializing all the walkers in the 𝒔0\bm{s}_{0} configuration.

V.2 Benchmark with Green function Monte Carlo

To control the accuracy of our calculation, we use two different methods. The first, internal to VMC, is to extrapolate the curve E​(var​[H]/E2)E(\text{var}[H]/E^{2}) versus var​[H]→0\text{var}[H]\to 0. It can be shown that the scaling close to the ground state should be linear [45]. Hence, we can use the energy variance pairs along the dynamical-χ\chi or dynamical-KK optimization, for the linear extrapolation (see Fig. 11 for an example). The difference between the extrapolation and the best VMC energy provides a good estimate of the error. This first method cannot distinguish the actual ground state from an excited state in case of e.g. a first order transition. The second method is to use the GFMC approach, a post VMC approach that projects the VMC ansatz onto the actual ground state of the system. GFMC is, in principle, exact. For the 1D model, we also have an independent exact calculation of the energy.

V.2.1 GFMC in a nutshell

GFMC is a lattice counterpart to the diffusion Monte Carlo approach [46]. Due to the presence of the lattice, GFMC can be formulated directly in the imaginary time continuum, without resorting to Trotterization or other discretization schemes. For completeness, we describe the method below and refer to the literature for the associated proofs [47, 48, 34, 35, 49]. The VMC ansatz plays an important underlying role in GFMC and, as we shall see, condition the quality of the results. We describe here the version corresponding to a fixed sign of the Hamiltonian matrix elements, i.e. H𝒔​𝒔′<0H_{\bm{s}\bm{s^{\prime}}}<0 for all off-diagonal elements adapted to the transverse field Ising model. In this case, the sign of the ground state wave function is known for each configuration (ψ𝒔≥0\psi_{\bm{s}}\geq 0, absence of sign problem). When this property is absent, either the method becomes strongly inefficient or one uses the so-called fixed-node approximation to restore it at the cost of a (difficult to control) approximation.

The goal of GFMC is to sample the state |ψ⁡(τ)⟩=e−H​τ​|ψ⟩|\psi(\tau)\rangle=e^{-H\tau}|\psi\rangle starting from the state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle represented by the VMC ansatz ψ\psi. For τ\tau large enough, |ψ⁡(τ)⟩|\psi(\tau)\rangle converges to the actual ground state |ψ0⟩|\psi^{0}\rangle of HH (in principle, for any choice of ψ\psi not orthogonal to ψ0\psi^{0}). The role of ψ\psi is both to be the starting point of the calculation but also to constrain the exploration of the configuration space. Hence, in the context of GFMC, ψ\psi is known as the ”guiding” wave function. The primary output of GFMC is the curve E⁡(τ)E(\tau) which starts at the VMC energy EE at τ=0\tau=0 and decreases toward E0E^{0}:

E⁡(τ)=⟨ψ|H​e−H​τ|ψ⟩⟨ψ|e−H​τ|ψ⟩.E(\tau)=\frac{\langle\psi|He^{-H\tau}|\psi\rangle}{\langle\psi|e^{-H\tau}|\psi\rangle}. (25)

A secondary outcome of GFMC is the area κ\kappa [see Fig. 12(a)] under the curve E⁡(τ)E(\tau),

κ=∫[E⁡(τ)−E0]​𝑑τ,\kappa=\int\ [E(\tau)-E^{0}]d\tau, (26)

which is a very good metric for the quality of the variational ansatz. Indeed, it can be shown [50] that the overlap Ω\Omega between |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle and |ψ0⟩|\psi^{0}\rangle (the so-called fidelity) is given by

Ω≡|⟨ψ|ψ0⟩|2⟨ψ|ψ⟩​⟨ψ0|ψ0⟩=e−κ.\Omega\equiv\frac{|\langle\psi|\psi^{0}\rangle|^{2}}{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\psi^{0}|\psi^{0}\rangle}=e^{-\kappa}. (27)

A good approximation of this area κ~\tilde{\kappa} is [50] (see Fig. 12b),

κ~≡(E⁡(0)−E0)2/2​var​[H]≈κ.\tilde{\kappa}\equiv(E(0)-E^{0})^{2}/2\text{var}[H]\approx\kappa. (28)

κ~\tilde{\kappa} is closely related to the VV-score which provides a justification for the success of the later as a metric for the quality of the wave function.

The algorithm uses a set of MM walkers, each corresponding to a configuration 𝒔α​(τ){\bm{s}}^{\alpha}(\tau) with α=1​…​M\alpha=1...M. Initially, the walkers must be distributed according to |ψ|2|\psi|^{2}. Each walker makes moves at discrete times distributed according to a Poisson statistics: the time tt that separates two moves is distributed according to

p⁡(t)=(H𝒔α​𝒔α−e𝒔α)​exp⁡[−(H𝒔α​𝒔α−e𝒔α)​t],p(t)=(H_{{\bm{s}}^{\alpha}{\bm{s}}^{\alpha}}-e_{{\bm{s}}^{\alpha}})\exp\left[-(H_{{\bm{s}}^{\alpha}{\bm{s}}^{\alpha}}-e_{{\bm{s}}^{\alpha}})t\right], (29)

which can be sampled directly. At each move, one of the spins is flipped. The choice of which of the VV spins is flipped is done according to

p𝒔′=ψ𝒔′∑𝒔​"ψ𝒔​"p_{\bm{s^{\prime}}}=\frac{\psi_{\bm{s^{\prime}}}}{\sum_{\bm{s"}}\psi_{\bm{s"}}} (30)

where the sum ∑𝒔​"\sum_{\bm{s"}} extends to all the configurations connected to 𝒔α​(τ){\bm{s}}^{\alpha}(\tau) by a single spin flip. At this point, the algorithm actually samples the VMC distribution |ψ|2|\psi|^{2}, it is a rejection free alternative to the Metropolis algorithm. To correct from the fact that one wants to sample from the actual ground state distribution |ψ0|2|\psi^{0}|^{2}, one assigns a weight wαw^{\alpha} to each walker. The weights are initialized to wα​(0)=1w^{\alpha}(0)=1. After a move, each weight is updated to

wα​(τ+t)=wα​(τ)​exp⁡(−e𝒔α​(τ)​t).w^{\alpha}(\tau+t)=w^{\alpha}(\tau)\exp( -e_{\boldsymbol{s}^\alpha(\tau)} t). (31)

The estimator of the energy is the weighted average,

E⁡(τ)≈∑αe𝒔α​(τ)​wα​(τ)∑αwα​(τ).E(\tau)\approx\frac{\sum_{\alpha}e_{{\bm{s}}^{\alpha}(\tau)}w^{\alpha}(\tau)}{\sum_{\alpha}w^{\alpha}(\tau)}. (32)

The above algorithm is exact (in the limit of large MM) but inefficient because a handful of the walkers’ weights will eventually become much larger than the others and dominate the average. Hence, this algorithm is completed with the so-called stochastic reconfiguration [34, 35] (same name, but not exactly the same mathematics as the one described in the first part of this manuscript). At fixed intervals, one performs the following ”death and spawn” algorithm where some walkers are removed and others are duplicated while maintaining a fixed total number MM of walkers: one calculates pα=M​wα/∑α′wα′p_{\alpha}=Mw^{\alpha}/\sum_{\alpha^{\prime}}w^{\alpha^{\prime}}. Writing pαp_{\alpha} as the sum of its floor and fractional part, pα=⌊pα⌋+δ​pαp_{\alpha}=\lfloor p_{\alpha}\rfloor+\delta p_{\alpha}, then ⌊pα⌋\lfloor p_{\alpha}\rfloor copies of walker α\alpha are created (i.e a walker with pα>1p_{\alpha}>1 is certain to survive). One selects the remaining M−∑α⌊pα⌋M-\sum_{\alpha}\lfloor p_{\alpha}\rfloor walkers according to the probability δ​pα\delta p_{\alpha} (i.e. a walker with pα<1p_{\alpha}<1 may die). This stochastic reconfiguration introduces some correlations between different walkers while keeping the joint probability for (𝒔α,wα)({\bm{s}}^{\alpha},w^{\alpha}) unaffected. This concludes the algorithm.

V.2.2 Benchmark for the one-dimensional model

The inset of Fig. 12(a) shows an example of VMC optimization for the 1D model (black line). During the optimization, we perform many GFMC calculations (green points). We find consistently that GFMC improves the accuracy by one or two orders of magnitude until the VMC ansatz is so close to the ground state that one is dominated by statistical fluctuations. Main Fig. 12(a) shows an example of the E⁡(τ)E(\tau) using a very bad (almost constant) variational ansatz. We find that for this small system, GFMC is capable to converge to the ground-state energy nevertheless. For this simple case, we also calculated the exact curve E⁡(τ)E(\tau) as a reference (black). The area κ\kappa corresponds to the shaded area and is directly linked to −log⁡Ω-\log\Omega. Figure 12(b) shows that a numerical integration of the E⁡(τ)E(\tau) curve obtained in GFMC actually provides the correct fidelity Ω\Omega. Also the proxy κ~\tilde{\kappa}, which can be computed without GFMC, provides a correct (but more approximate) estimate of the overlap.

We used the 1D model also for comparing the performances of the MPS, the trivial PN consisting of two identical MPS, and the corresponding SBS limit. Our results for hx=1h_{x}=1 are summarized in Fig. 13. We find that even for the 1D case, which is known to be very favorable to MPS, the PN ansatz consistently performs better than MPS by almost 2 digits. However, the PN ansatz is not better than the SBS limit (except at χ=3\chi=3, a point for which the meta-parameters α\alpha, ϵ1\epsilon_{1}, initialization, etc., have been optimized much more aggressively compared to the rest of the curve).

V.2.3 Benchmark for the two-dimensional model

In this section, we present our reference calculations for the 2D model. We have performed various GFMC runs for different ansätze and values of hxh_{x} and checked the consistency of the results. We have also, for completeness, compared the results with what could be obtained from a zero variance extrapolation [45, 51, 17] (see Fig. 11 for an example) and with the result of a regular MPS ansatz, as used in DMRG. The obtained values are the reference energies E0E^{0} used throughout this manuscript to estimate errors. A sample of our most precise energies are presented in Table 1. At small values of hx=1,1.5h_{x}=1,1.5 the acceptance rate of the naïve Metropolis algorithm decreased leading to an increase of the auto-correlation time of the Markov process. In that regime, we switched to a rejection free sampling algorithm. In practice, the rejection free sampling is obtained by using GFMC in a mode where we force the weights of all walkers to remain equal to 11 at all times.

In the process of elaborating this benchmark, we have made two important remarks. First, that the VV-score is, at least for this model, a very good proxy for the relative precision on the energy [see Fig. 14(a)] as well as the overlap κ~\tilde{\kappa} [see Fig. 14(b)].

The second point is that the GFMC results are very robust, as long as ψ\psi and ψ0\psi^{0} are in the same phase (antiferromagnet versus paramagnet). This is illustrated very clearly in Fig. 15 which shows the error of the energy estimate as a function of hxh_{x} (the actual hxh_{x} of the Hamiltonian in the GFMC run) and hx′h_{x}^{\prime} (the value of the transverse field that was used in the VMC optimization to construct the guiding wave function). In other words, in Fig. 15, we have used ”bad” guiding wave functions that have been optimized for a wrong value of the transverse field hx′≠hxh_{x}^{\prime}\neq h_{x}. The energies in Fig. 15 were averaged over the window τ∈[4,6]\tau\in[4,6], and over τ∈[2,6]\tau\in[2,6] on the diagonal. Random walks were performed using 32000 walkers and reconfiguration every Δ​τ=0.1\Delta\tau=0.1.

We see that both hxh_{x} and hx′h_{x}^{\prime} must be in the same sector (i.e. same side with respect to the critical value hx=2.3h_{x}=2.3) for GFMC to succeed (blue region). In the antiferromagnetic sector, we observe an additional triangular structure which shows that the variational ansatz must be less localized than the true ground state; otherwise certain configurations are simply never visited.

V.3 Stochastic reconfiguration versus normalized gradient descent

Figure 16 shows the result of the optimization for the PN ansatz (red) and in the SBS limit (blue) without SR (left panel) and with SR (right panel). We find that the optimization in the SBS limit is much more robust than for the PN ansatz, as a good accuracy can be reached even using the normalized gradient descent. However, SR is consistently more accurate and does not require a fine tuning of the α\alpha parameter. We recall that, in our scheme, there is no additional cost to using SR since we only optimize a small number of parameters at a given time (in contrast to usual gradient descent where all parameters are optimized simultaneously). In the same spirit, Fig. 17 shows different optimization paths using/not using SR and using/not using dynamical-KK optimization. The optimization is globally very robust to these changes.

V.4 Robustness of the optimization with respect to the presence of nonlinearities in the ansatz

We have found empirically that increasing the value of dd, i.e. making the perceptrain more non-linear, makes the optimization less stable. This is illustrated in Fig. 18, which contrasts d=2d=2 with d=5d=5: the d=5d=5 results are consistently less precise than d=2d=2 and the optimization becomes unstable at a smaller rank (χ=6\chi=6 instead of χ=7\chi=7). In principle the d=5d=5 ansatz contains the full subspace of the d=2d=2 one. Hence we conclude that the poor results obtained for d=5d=5 are associated with an energy landscape that becomes harder to navigate. We attribute this difficulty to optimize to an inefficiency of the additional parameters introduced: they do not provide significant extra expressivity but make the energy landscape harder to navigate. Altogether, it seems that the SBS limit with a large value of KK is a good compromise.

We also observed that in the limit of small hxh_{x}, where the ground state converges to a product state and should therefore be well approximated by a low rank MPS (χ=1\chi=1 is exact in the limit of hx=0h_{x}=0), the optimization becomes unstable earlier. We find that when the rank is increased above χ=2\chi=2, both MPS and SBS errors become large in a manner reminiscent of Fig. 18 (not shown). Again, we attribute this instability to the energy landscape being harder to navigate.

VI Conclusions

In this work, we have explored how a simple network of ”perceptrains,” i.e. a neural network whose neuron units have been replaced by matrix product states, can be used to construct a variational ansatz for the 2D transverse field Ising model. We have learned a number of important lessons:

  • •

    First, the ansatz is accurate (typically five digits) for the entire range of transverse fields using ranks that would be considered as ”tiny” in the tensor network community. This is very promising.

  • •

    Second, a local optimization strategy, reminiscent of the one of the DMRG algorithm, provides a robust path to the ground state. This is also very important as variational approaches can be easily plagued by the difficulty to optimize (local minimum, barren plateaus…)

  • •

    Third, the ability to change the number of parameters dynamically during the optimization is very relevant. It serves both to stabilize the optimization in presence of the (VMC induced) noise but also to use an optimal number of variational parameters. Overall, we obtain a very stable optimization.

  • •

    Fourth, the main strength of our ansatz comes from the children MPS, not the master perceptrain. Indeed, the SBS limit, with the master MPS at χ=1\chi=1, and very limited expressive power, reaches the accuracy similar to the one of the full ansatz. Each of these child MPS can be seen as a complex “feature” capturing the correlations along certain directions (for example horizontal or vertical).

We believe that these features make perceptrain networks very strong candidates to challenge (or be combined with) regular neural networks for many-body ansatz and perhaps be useful in other contexts as well.

On the physics side, we could essentially solve the two dimensional transverse field Ising model on a square lattice. The model is relevant for describing lattices of atoms in a superposition of ground and Rydberg states. Since the Rydberg platform has been proffered as a solver for discrete optimization problems, we can use our results to put bounds on the performance needed to reach the so-called quantum advantage.

Future works will explore different directions. First, our technique is directly applicable to more complex models of quantum magnetism or fermionic models, such as the Hubbard model. This requires a straightforward generalization from real to complex wave functions which, our preliminary results indicate, should not be problematic. The performance of the present approach should certainly be explored in these models. Second, further technical aspects can be improved: local optimization should allow one to use tailored optimization to speed up convergence; the choice of the orderings could be optimized and integrated in the optimization algorithm; one could use more expressive tensor networks, such as tensor trees [52, 53] at no additional cost; one could build deeper and wider perceptrain networks. Third, the ansatz could also be used for studying the actual dynamics of the problem, within the time-dependent variational principle formalism.
